1.topic: Spreadsheet layout, number formats and file types
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. use alignment, wrap text and merge and centre to lay out a spreadsheet;
2. apply number formats (currency, percentage, decimals) correctly;
3. save a spreadsheet in a suitable file type (.xlsx, .csv, .pdf);
4. retrieve a saved file and name versions sensibly.

## Materials

Computers with Excel or an equivalent, a projector, and a printed school fees record with five learners.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show a fees table where the title is squeezed in one cell, the numbers are left-aligned and a long heading is cut off. Ask the class to say what they would change.

## Development

1. Revise selecting cells and formatting the heading row.
2. Alignment: text to the left, numbers to the right so the digits line up.
3. Wrap Text makes a long heading fit in a cell by using more than one line.
4. Merge and Centre joins several cells into one, used for a table title.
5. Decimal places and currency: 250 typed in a cell can be shown as ₦250.00.
6. Percentage: 0.4 shows as 40%. Explain that the cell still holds 0.4.
7. File types: .xlsx keeps formulas and formatting; .csv is plain text with commas and loses formatting; .pdf is for printing and reading only.
8. Version names: Fees_JSS2, Fees_JSS2_v2.

## Class activity

Pupils lay out the fees record, apply formats and save it as .xlsx and as .pdf. They compare the two files.

## Evaluation

1. When would you save as .csv instead of .xlsx?
2. Why is 0.4 shown as 40%?

## Assignment

Worksheet on the app.

reading.title: Laying out a spreadsheet and choosing the file type
reading.content:
# Spreadsheet layout, number formats and file types

In JSS1 you learned to make a spreadsheet and to format a heading row. A spreadsheet that other people read must also be **laid out well**, show numbers in the **right format**, and be **saved in the right file type**.

## Layout

**Alignment.** Text is normally on the left. Numbers are best on the **right**, so that units line up under units and tens under tens. This makes a column of money easy to compare.

**Wrap Text.** A long heading such as *Amount paid for the term* can be cut off. Wrap Text breaks it into two or more lines inside the cell, so the whole heading can be read.

**Merge and Centre.** This joins several cells into one big cell and centres the words in it. It is used for the **title** at the top of a table.

## Number formats

The format changes the way a number is shown, not the number itself.

| Value in cell | Format | Shown |
|---|---|---|
| 250 | Currency | ₦250.00 |
| 3.5 | Number, 0 decimals | 4 (rounded for display) |
| 0.4 | Percentage | 40% |
| 12 × 250 | Currency | ₦3,000.00 |

Note that 0.4 means 40 out of 100. The percentage format multiplies it by 100 and adds the % sign.

## File types

When you save, choose a file type that suits the job.

- **.xlsx (Excel Workbook)**: keeps your formulas, formats and charts. Use this while you are still working.
- **.csv (comma separated values)**: plain text with commas between the entries. It keeps the data only, no colours or formulas. Many programs can read it, so it is used for moving data from one program to another.
- **.pdf**: a fixed copy for reading and printing. The reader cannot easily change it. Send this when you only want someone to read.

## Naming versions

Name files so that you know which is newest: *Fees_JSS2.xlsx*, then *Fees_JSS2_v2.xlsx*. Do not call every file *Book1*.

## Worked example

A tuckshop sells 12 bags of pure water at ₦250 each. In B2 put 12 and in C2 put 250. In D2 type **=B2*C2**, which gives 3000. Select D2 and choose Currency, and it shows **₦3,000.00**. The title in row 1 is merged across A1 to D1 and centred.

2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. plan a presentation with a storyboard before opening the software;
2. use a theme and layouts so that all slides look the same;
3. add and arrange slides, and use speaker notes;
4. judge a slide and say how to improve it.

## Materials

Computers with PowerPoint or an equivalent, a projector, plain paper for storyboards, and two printed example slides (one good, one poor).

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show a poor slide with 80 words in small size, red text on a green background. Ask pupils to count what is wrong with it.

## Development

1. Plan first: purpose, audience, number of slides. Draw a storyboard with a box for each slide.
2. Choose one theme. The theme sets colours and fonts for all slides, so the presentation looks tidy.
3. Choose a layout for each slide to suit its content: Title, Title and Content, Two Content, Blank.
4. Slide Sorter view: drag slides to change the order, duplicate a slide, delete a slide.
5. Speaker notes: type what you will say in the notes area. The audience does not see them.
6. Improve a poor slide: cut words, increase letter size, change colours, split one slide into two.

## Class activity

Pupils draw a five-slide storyboard on "Road safety in my town" and then build it in the software.

## Evaluation

1. What does a storyboard help you to do?
2. How do speaker notes help the presenter?

## Assignment

Quiz on the app.

reading.title: From a plan to a tidy presentation
reading.content:
# Planning and designing a presentation

In JSS1 you made simple slides. Now we learn to make a presentation that a visitor would enjoy, by **planning before you open the computer**.

## Step 1: Plan

Ask three questions.

1. What is the **purpose**? (To teach, to persuade, to report?)
2. Who is the **audience**? (Classmates, parents, the principal?)
3. How many **slides** do I need? Do not make a slide for every sentence. Five to eight slides is enough for a short talk.

Then draw a **storyboard**. This is a row of boxes on paper, one for each slide, with a note about what each slide will contain. A storyboard helps you see the order of your ideas and saves time at the computer.

## Step 2: Choose a theme and layouts

A **theme** gives all the slides the same colours and fonts. Use **one** theme so the presentation looks like one piece of work. Pick a **layout** for each slide.

- **Title Slide** for the first slide.
- **Title and Content** for points.
- **Two Content** for comparing two things.
- **Blank** or **Picture** when a picture says more than words.

## Step 3: Arrange and edit

In **Slide Sorter** view you see all the slides in small boxes. Drag a slide to move it, copy a slide to **duplicate** it, or delete a slide you do not need.

## Step 4: Speaker notes

Under each slide is a notes area. You can type what you want to say. The audience does not see it. It helps you remember facts, so you do not need to put everything on the slide.

## Step 5: Check the design

A good slide has:
- a **clear heading**;
- **3 to 5 short points** (key words);
- **letters of size 24 or above**;
- **contrast** between the text and the background.

## Worked example: improving a slide

A pupil's slide on *Road safety* has 80 words in size 12, in red letters on a green background.

To improve it: split it into two slides, keep 4 short points on each (for example *Look left and right*, *Use the zebra crossing*), change the letters to size 28, and use dark letters on a light background. Move the extra facts into the speaker notes.

3.topic: Pictures, sound, video, transitions and animations
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. insert, resize and crop a picture on a slide;
2. add audio and a video clip to a slide;
3. tell a transition from an animation and apply each;
4. use effects in a way that helps, not distracts, the audience.

## Materials

Computers with PowerPoint or an equivalent, a folder with pictures, a short audio clip and a short video clip, and a projector.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show a slide with only words, and the same slide with one clear picture. Ask which helps the audience understand faster.

## Development

1. Insert, then Pictures, then choose a file. Resize by dragging a corner handle; dragging a side handle stretches the picture and spoils its shape.
2. Crop to remove parts you do not need.
3. Insert, then Audio, to add music or a recorded voice. Choose whether it plays automatically or on click. Video is added in the same way.
4. Keep the pictures, audio and video in the same folder as the presentation. If you move the file to another computer without them, they may not play.
5. A transition is the effect when one slide changes to the next (Fade, Push, Wipe). An animation is the effect on an object inside a slide, such as a bullet flying in.
6. Rules: use few effects, the same transition throughout, short clips, and animations only to show points one at a time.

## Class activity

Pupils add two pictures, one audio clip and one transition to a slide about "My school", and animate the bullet points to appear one by one.

## Evaluation

1. What is the difference between a transition and an animation?
2. Why must you drag a corner handle to resize a picture?

## Assignment

Problem set on the app.

reading.title: Making slides come alive, without making a mess
reading.content:
# Pictures, sound, video, transitions and animations

Pictures and sound can make a presentation clearer and more interesting. But too many effects can annoy the audience and hide the message. This lesson shows how to use them well.

## Pictures

To add a picture, click **Insert**, then **Pictures**, and choose the file.

- To **resize** a picture, drag one of the **corner handles**. This keeps the shape. If you drag a handle on the **side**, the picture is stretched and looks wrong.
- To **crop**, use the Crop tool to cut away the part you do not need.
- Choose a picture that **supports** the point. A picture of a pot of jollof rice helps a slide about food, but not a slide about the school library.

## Audio and video

Click **Insert**, then **Audio** or **Video**. You can add a recorded voice, music or a short clip. You choose whether it plays **automatically** or **when you click**.

Important: the file is not always stored inside the presentation. Keep the audio and video in the **same folder** as the presentation. If you copy only the presentation to another computer, the sound or video may not play.

## Transitions

A **transition** is the effect shown when one slide **changes to the next**. Examples are *Fade*, *Push* and *Wipe*. Choose one calm transition and use it on all slides.

## Animations

An **animation** is an effect on **an object inside one slide**, such as a picture, a heading or a bullet point. For example, you can make the bullet points *Fly in* one after the other, so the audience listens to one point at a time.

| | Transition | Animation |
|---|---|---|
| Happens | between two slides | inside one slide |
| Acts on | the whole slide | one object, such as a bullet |
| Example | Fade | Fly in |

## Good practice

- Use **few effects**; use the same transition on every slide.
- Keep clips **short**. A long video eats the time of your talk.
- Do not let the effect hide the words.
- Remember the file becomes **bigger** when it has many pictures and videos. It may be too large to send by email.

## Worked example

A pupil's slide on *Our school garden* has a photo, resized from a corner so it is not stretched; the three bullets *Plant seeds*, *Water daily*, *Pick vegetables* appear one by one with *Fly in*; and every slide changes with *Fade*.

reading.content:
# Printing and saving documents and presentations

A printer uses paper, ink and electricity. A careful user prints only what is needed, and in the right way. Saving in the right file format makes sure that your work can be opened by the person who needs it.

## The Print screen

Press **Ctrl+P** to open the Print screen. On the right is the **Print Preview**, which shows how each page will look on paper. Always check it before you print. A mistake you see in the preview costs nothing; a mistake on paper wastes a sheet.

## Print settings

**Copies.** The number of complete sets you want.

**Page range.** Which pages to print.
- *All pages*
- *A single page*: type 3
- *A range*: type 2-4 to print pages 2, 3 and 4 (three pages)
- *Separate pages*: type 1,5 to print page 1 and page 5

**Orientation.**
- *Portrait* is tall. It suits letters and essays.
- *Landscape* is wide. It suits wide tables and slides.

**Colour.** Black and white uses less ink and costs less.

## Handouts

A presentation of 12 slides printed one slide per page uses 12 sheets. As **handouts** you can print 3 or 6 slides on one sheet. With 6 per page, 12 slides need only 12 ÷ 6 = **2 sheets**. Pupils can write notes beside the slides on the 3-per-page handout.

## Choosing a file format

| Format | Ending | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Word document | .docx | you still want to edit the document |
| PowerPoint presentation | .pptx | you still want to edit or present the slides |
| PDF | .pdf | you want a fixed copy that looks the same on any device, to read, print or send |

To make a PDF, choose **Save As** and pick PDF as the type, or choose Print and select *Save as PDF*.

## Worked example

A teacher needs 30 copies of a 5-page notice. The paper needed is 5 × 30 = **150 sheets**. If she prints on both sides, she uses 150 ÷ 2 = **75 sheets**. If one sheet costs ₦10, the cost drops from ₦1,500 to ₦750.

Before sending the notice to parents by WhatsApp, she saves it as **PDF**, so the layout does not change on their phones.

reading.title: What the internet is, and how we use it
reading.content:
# The internet, browsers and search engines

## What is the internet?

The **internet** is a huge network of computer networks joined together all over the world. Because they are joined, a computer in Ibadan can fetch information from a computer in another country in a few seconds.

## How do we connect?

You need three things:

1. A **device**: a phone, tablet or computer.
2. A **connection** from an **Internet Service Provider (ISP)**. In Nigeria, mobile data from companies such as MTN, Airtel or Glo, or a fibre or Wi-Fi line.
3. **Data** or a Wi-Fi password so that the device is allowed to use that connection.

## Uses of the internet

- **Communication**: email, messages and video calls.
- **Research and learning**: finding facts, watching lessons, reading books.
- **Entertainment**: music, films, games.
- **Business**: shopping online, mobile banking, advertising.
- **News**: reading about what is happening now.

## The internet and the web

People often say "internet" when they mean the "web". They are not the same. The **internet** is the network. The **World Wide Web** (WWW) is a collection of web pages that are carried on the internet. Email and video calls also use the internet, but they are not web pages.

## Browser and search engine

A **web browser** is a program on your device that **opens and shows web pages**. Examples are Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge and Safari.

A **search engine** is a **website that helps you find** pages on a topic. Examples are Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo. You open a browser first, then go to a search engine, type your question and read the results.

| | Web browser | Search engine |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A program | A website |
| What it does | Opens web pages | Finds web pages |
| Example | Chrome | Google |

## The web address (URL)

Every page has an address called a **URL**. Look at **https://www.unilag.edu.ng/admissions**.

- **https** is the protocol, and the **s** means the connection is secure.
- **www.unilag.edu.ng** is the domain name, the name of the website.
- **.edu.ng** ends the name: *edu* is for education and *ng* is for Nigeria.
- **/admissions** is the page inside the website.

Other endings are **.gov.ng** (Nigerian government), **.org** (organisations) and **.com** (business).

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. choose good keywords and use quotation marks to search;
2. judge whether a source can be trusted;
3. write a simple citation for a source they use;
4. avoid copying and pasting without credit.

## Materials

A computer with internet access, a projector, and a printout of two web pages on the same topic (one reliable, one poor).

3. Use quotation marks to search for an exact phrase, for example "harmattan dust".
4. Add a word to narrow a search (flood Lagos causes). Change the words if the results are poor.
5. Judge the source with four questions: Who wrote it? When was it written? Why was it written (to inform, to sell, to persuade)? Do other good sources agree?
6. Signs of a reliable source: a named author or organisation, a recent date, endings such as .gov.ng or .edu.ng, facts that other sources support. Signs of a poor source: no author, no date, too many adverts, shocking claims.
7. Cite the source: author or website, title, website name, date and URL. Never copy and paste without credit.

reading.title: Finding good information and giving credit
reading.content:
# Searching well, judging sources and citing

Anyone can find thousands of pages on a topic in seconds. The skill is to find the **right** ones, decide which to **trust**, and **give credit** to the people whose work you use.

## Searching well

**Think first.** Ask yourself what exactly you want to know.

**Use keywords, not long sentences.** A search engine reads your words and looks for pages with them. Small words add noise.

- Weak search: *please tell me what are the causes of floods in Lagos state*
- Better search: *causes of flooding Lagos*

**Quotation marks** make the engine look for the **exact phrase**. Searching for *"harmattan dust"* finds pages with those two words together, in that order.

**Narrow or change.** Too many pages? Add a word, like *causes of flooding Lagos drainage*. Too few? Use a simpler or different word, such as *flood* instead of *deluge*.

## Judging a source

Not everything online is true. Ask four questions:

| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Who** wrote it? | A named expert or organisation is more reliable than "Anonymous". |
| **When** was it written? | Old pages may be out of date. |
| **Why** was it written? | To inform, to sell something or to persuade? |
| **Do others agree?** | Check the facts in at least two good sources. |

Signs of a **reliable** source: a named author, a recent date, a trusted ending such as *.gov.ng* or *.edu.ng*, and facts that other sources support.

Signs of a **poor** source: no author, no date, many adverts, and a shocking claim with no proof.

## Citing sources

To **cite** is to say where your information came from. This is fair to the writer, and it lets your teacher check your facts. A simple citation gives:

- the author or website,
- the title of the page,
- the website name,
- the date, and
- the web address (URL).

**Example:** Nigerian Meteorological Agency. *Seasonal climate outlook.* NiMet website, 2025. https://nimet.gov.ng.

## Copy and paste

Copying a writer's sentences and presenting them as your own is **plagiarism**. Read, understand, and write in your own words, and cite where you found it.

## Worked example

A pupil searching for causes of flooding in Lagos finds two pages. One is from a state environment ministry, with a named author and a date from last year. The other has no author, a date from nine years ago, and many adverts. She chooses the first one and cites it.

reading.content:
# Email: composing, sending and managing

**Email** is short for **electronic mail**. It is a message you send over the internet to another person's mailbox. It arrives in seconds, even if the person is in another country. Schools, banks and businesses use email for official messages.

## The email address

An email address looks like **ngozi.okeke@example.com**.

- **ngozi.okeke** is the user name.
- **@** is read as "at".
- **example.com** is the mail provider.

An address has no spaces and uses only one @. Choose a sensible user name, because it will be seen by teachers and employers.

## Parts of a new email

| Part | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **To** | The main person who must receive the message |
| **Cc** | Carbon copy: a copy for someone who should know. Everyone can see who is in Cc. |
| **Bcc** | Blind carbon copy: a hidden copy. Others cannot see who is in Bcc. |
| **Subject** | A short title that tells what the message is about |
| **Body** | The message itself |
| **Attachment** | A file such as a document or picture sent with the email |

## Reply, Reply All and Forward

- **Reply** goes back to the sender only.
- **Reply All** goes to the sender and everyone else on the message. Use it only when everyone needs your answer. Using it by mistake can send private replies to many people.
- **Forward** sends the message to someone new.

## The mailbox

- **Inbox**: messages you receive.
- **Sent**: messages you have sent.
- **Drafts**: messages you started but have not sent.
- **Spam**: unwanted or suspicious messages. Do not click on links in them.
- **Trash**: deleted messages.

## Writing a good email

1. Write a **clear subject**, such as *Date of the JSS2 quiz*, not *Hello* or no subject.
2. Begin with a **greeting**: *Dear Mr Bello,*
3. Keep the message **short and polite**, with correct spelling.
4. End with a **sign-off**: *Yours faithfully, Chioma Eze, JSS2A*.
5. Do not WRITE IN CAPITAL LETTERS, because it looks like shouting.
6. Mention the attachment, and attach it before you press Send.

## Safety

Do not open an attachment or click a link from someone you do not know. It may carry a virus.

## Worked example

**To:** mr.bello@example.com
**Subject:** Date of the JSS2 quiz
**Body:** Dear Mr Bello, Please could you tell me the date of the JSS2 Digital Technologies quiz? I have attached my revision notes. Thank you. Chioma Eze, JSS2A.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. make and keep a strong password;
2. say what cyberbullying is and what to do about it;
3. name types of malware and how they spread;
4. list ways to protect a device from malware.

## Materials

A projector, cards with sample passwords (weak and strong), and a short role-play script about an unkind message in a class group chat.

## Starter (5 minutes)

1. A password protects your account. Strong password: at least 12 characters, mixing capital and small letters, numbers and symbols, and not a name, a birthday or "password123". A passphrase of several unrelated words is easy to remember and strong.
2. Keep it safe: do not share it, use a different password for each account, do not write it where others can see it, and use two-step verification if the site offers it.
3. Cyberbullying is using phones or the internet to hurt, shame or frighten someone. If it happens: do not reply, save the messages as proof, block the person, and tell a trusted adult. If you see it happening to another, do not join in or forward it.
4. Malware is harmful software. Virus (attaches to files and spreads), worm (spreads itself over a network), trojan (looks useful but is harmful), spyware (secretly watches), ransomware (locks files and demands money).
5. Protection: antivirus, updates, do not open unknown attachments, avoid pirated software, scan flash drives, back up files.

## Class activity

Pupils rate five sample passwords and fix the weak ones, then act out what to do when a rude message arrives in a group chat.

reading.content:
# Staying safe online: passwords, bullying and malware

The internet is useful, but it also has people and programs that want to harm you. A few good habits will keep you and your device safe.

## Passwords

A **password** is a secret word that proves you are the owner of an account. If someone else knows it, they can read your messages and pretend to be you.

**A strong password:**
- has **at least 12 characters**;
- mixes **capital and small letters, numbers and symbols**;
- is **not** a name, date of birth, phone number, or something easy like *password123* or *12345678*;
- is **different** for each account. If one account is hacked, the others stay safe.

An easy way is a **passphrase**: several unrelated words and a number, such as *Mango!Drum7Window*.

**Keep it secret.** Do not share it with friends, do not leave it on paper where others can see it, and use **two-step verification** when it is offered. With two-step verification, a code is sent to your phone as well, so a thief with only your password cannot get in.

## Cyberbullying

**Cyberbullying** is using phones, social media or messages to hurt, shame or frighten another person. It can be rude messages, spreading rumours, sharing embarrassing photos or leaving someone out on purpose. Words online can hurt as much as words said face to face, and they can spread quickly.

**If it happens to you:**
1. Do **not** reply in anger.
2. **Save** the messages or take screenshots as proof.
3. **Block** the person.
4. **Tell** a trusted adult: a parent, a teacher or the school counsellor.

**If you see it happening to another person,** do not join in, do not forward the message, and tell an adult.

## Malware

**Malware** is software made to do harm. Common types:

| Type | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Virus** | Attaches to a file or program and spreads when that file is opened or shared |
| **Worm** | Spreads by itself across a network |
| **Trojan** | Looks like a useful program, but does harm once it is installed |
| **Spyware** | Secretly watches what you do and collects your information |
| **Ransomware** | Locks your files and demands money to open them |

Malware spreads through **email attachments, unknown links, pirated software, infected flash drives** and fake websites.

## Protecting a device

- Install **antivirus** software and keep it up to date.
- Install **updates** to the system and the apps.
- Do **not** open attachments or click links from people you do not know.
- **Scan** a flash drive before opening it.
- **Back up** important files, so a loss does not destroy your work.

## Worked example

Chidera receives a message: *Your phone has a virus! Click here to clean it now.* This is likely a trick. She does not click. She tells her mother, and her phone's own antivirus app is used to check it.

1. Ethics are ideas about what is right and wrong. Digital ethics apply them to computers and the internet.
2. Intellectual property is something a person created with the mind: a song, a story, a drawing, a program. The owner has rights over it.
3. Copyright is the legal right of the creator to control copying and use. Using someone's work without permission can be stealing and against the law. Pirating films, music and software is an example.
4. Some work may be used with permission or credit. Some authors share work freely under licences such as Creative Commons. Check what is allowed and give credit.

reading.content:
# Digital ethics: copyright, plagiarism and social media

**Ethics** are ideas about what is right and what is wrong. **Digital ethics** apply those ideas to computers, phones and the internet. Something being easy to do online does not make it right.

## Intellectual property and copyright

**Intellectual property** is something a person has created with their mind: a song, a story, a photograph, a drawing, a computer program. The creator owns it, just as you own your school bag.

**Copyright** is the legal right of the creator to say who can copy, sell or share the work. If you copy and share a musician's song or a film without permission, you take away the money the creator should earn. This is called **piracy**, and it is against the law in Nigeria and many countries.

Some creators allow others to use their work for free if they follow certain rules. For example, a photograph may carry a **Creative Commons** licence that lets you use it if you give credit to the photographer. Always check what the owner allows.

## Plagiarism

**Plagiarism** is presenting another person's work or ideas as your own. It may be copying sentences from a website, copying a friend's homework, or buying an essay.

To avoid plagiarism:
1. Read and understand the source.
2. Write the idea **in your own words**.
3. **Cite** the source.
4. If you use the exact words, put them in quotation marks and name the writer.

Plagiarism is a kind of cheating. It also stops you from learning.

## Using social media responsibly

Social media can spread kindness and knowledge, but also harm.

- **Think before you post.** A post can be seen by many people and may stay online for a long time.
- **Keep private information private**: your address, phone number and school timetable.
- **Ask permission** before posting a photo or video of another person.
- **Check before you share.** Fake news spreads quickly. Look at who wrote it and whether trusted sources say the same.
- **Be kind.** Do not insult, bully or mock others.
- **Be honest.** Do not pretend to be someone else.

## Worked example

A pupil finds a drawing of a lion on a website and puts it in her project, saying she drew it. This is wrong because it is someone else's work, presented as hers. The right way is to say who drew it and where she found it, or to draw her own.
